hints: Focus on the two separate jobs here, temperature controls the shape of the distribution, while a catalyst controls the activation energy.
The temperature is kept constant, so the distribution of molecular energies and the height of peak P cannot change.
A catalyst provides a route of lower activation energy, so think about which way the $E_a$ mark must shift to give a larger shaded area.
walkthrough:
**Understand what peak P shows**

Think of the curve as showing how energy is shared out between molecules at one temperature. Peak P is the most probable energy, and its height and position depend only on temperature.

Rule: constant $T$ means same distribution, same P.

**Understand what a catalyst does**

A catalyst does not heat or cool the gas and does not give molecules more energy. It provides an alternative pathway with a lower activation energy, $E_a$.

Effect: $$E_{a}(catalysed) < E_{a}(uncatalysed)$$

**Combine the two ideas**

Because $T$ is constant, the curve stays exactly where it is, so P is the same. Because $E_a$ is smaller, the $E_a$ line moves to the left to a lower energy value.

That left shift makes the shaded area beyond $E_a$ bigger, so a greater proportion of molecules can react.

options.A: Incorrect. The $E_a$ moving left is right for a catalyst, but peak P getting lower is wrong. A lower, flatter peak happens when temperature is increased, not when a catalyst is added at constant temperature.
options.B: Incorrect on both parts. Peak P stays the same because temperature is constant, and $E_a$ moves left, not right. Moving right would mean a higher activation energy, which would slow the reaction down.
options.C: Correct. Temperature is constant so the Boltzmann distribution is unchanged and peak P stays the same. The catalyst lowers $E_a$, so the $E_a$ line moves left and more molecules have energy >= $E_a$.
options.D: Incorrect. Peak P staying the same is right, but $E_a$ moving right is wrong. A shift to the right means increased activation energy, the opposite of catalytic action.
